items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The saxophones were Marshall Royal, Frank Wess, Ernie Wilkins, Charlie Fowlkes on baritone, and myself.

ctx.x: When you joined the band who was there at that point?

In the trumpet section were Joe Newman, a gentleman by the name of Paul Campbell -- they used to call him Uncle Cam -- Wendell Culley, a very distinguished looking and acting person from Worchester, Mass., who spoke perfect English and was a gentleman and always wore a suit and tie. I said Joe Newman, right? The lead trumpeter was a person called Renauld Jones. Trombones were Henry Coker, Benny Powell, and the composer-arranger Johnny Mandel. The saxophones were Marshall Royal, Frank Wess, Ernie Wilkins, Charlie…
So at that point Jimmy Wilkins had left the band?

items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: the saxophone section at that time was excellent with Marshall Royal playing lead, Frank Wess playing either alto or the other tenor, and Charlie Fowlkes playing baritone.

ctx.x: Well that was a problem that existed the entire eleven years I was with the band. I never had the feeling that I really fit, except on uptempo songs. I was trying to fill Lester Young’s shoes, and really was not making it, to my way of thinking. I mean I was

reading the music, no problem reading and interpreting the music, and the saxophone section at that time was excellent with Marshall Royal playing lead, Frank Wess playing either alto or the other tenor, and Charlie Fowlkes playing baritone. The second alto chair was the only chair that just fluctuated all throughout the entire time I was there. So I fit into the section very well, because I loved big band music and playing in the section and all that. But soloing I always felt that I fell a little short of what…
Did you get stuck with that then a little bit?

items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: So Frank Wess was getting prepared to take my solo, ‘cause ostensibly I hadn’t shown yet.

ctx.x: The band refused to play for him. And Basie died. And he was looking at him like “I told you.”

There was a time in Chicago when we played, it was a Birdland show, we played at the opera house, and the concert started at 8:00. And I’d had company that afternoon at the hotel, and at 8:00 I was just waking up, and the band was playing, no Frank Foster. So I hurriedly got dressed and called a taxi down to the theater, and I had got there just in time to miss the first half. So I walked in after the intermission was over, and hurriedly got my horn out. In the meantime, the first song after intermission was a…

items.title: Frank Wess interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995
items.q: You and Frank Foster were on the band—

ctx.x: Oh, I can’t. I don’t know. I really can’t remember.
Was there a certain etiquette among the players about getting the solos? How did you decide between you. You and Frank Foster were on the band—
Well that’s up to the band leader.
